title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) comparing a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) pipeline against accepting an LLM suggestion directly for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and deterministic validator, we sampled K=200 paired tasks and produced a single shared generator output per intent (shared_initial_generation) evaluated in both arms. Requested_model = gpt-5-mini. Observed primary outcome: baseline = 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; guarded (G→V→R) = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair loop was never invoked. We release the full preregistration, raw model/provider traces, validator traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts (SHA‑256s recorded) to enable exact replay. We interpret the null as a ceiling case under the chosen task/model/validator regime and discuss design implications for future confirmatory evaluations that aim to demonstrate verifier/repair utility in realistic, failure‑rich settings.

sections.introduction: Automating NetOps intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises accelerated change cycles but raises operational safety concerns: generated changes can introduce reachability regressions or outages. A common mitigation pattern is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): an LLM proposes a configuration, a deterministic verifier checks invariants (reachability, ordering, group constraints), and an automated repair attempt corrects violations. While multiple prior works and benchmarks advocate this pipeline, the marginal benefit of inserting a verifier+repair layer depends fundamentally on the generator error profile, validator coverage, and task distribution. To provide a reproducible causal estimate under strict experimental governance, we preregistered a paired design that holds the generator output fixed between arms (shared_initial_generation), ensuring that any difference in final validator outcome is attributable solely to the verifier+repair machinery. Our run is fully artifact‑grounded: preregistration (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop), provider traces, scoring traces, and execution manifest are archived with SHA‑256 hashes for exact replay.
sections.related_work: Recent literature on LLMs for NetOps and AIOps converges on two directions: (i) building end‑to‑end agentic workflows that use verification and bounded tool use to increase operational reliability, and (ii) constructing benchmarks that functionally evaluate LLM proposals against formal or emulator‑based validators (e.g., Cornetto and related generate‑validate‑repair studies). Position papers have emphasized confining LLMs to translation and relying on deterministic solvers for long‑horizon reasoning. Our work differs: it is a preregistered, paired confirmatory experiment that isolates the verifier marginal effect by fixing the generator output (shared_initial_generation) and publishing exact per‑episode validator traces to support independent reanalysis. Representative verified literature that motivated our design and context is cited in the artifacts (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The study preregistration (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256 archived) froze the research question, sampling plan, estimand, and analysis prior to execution. Primary confirmatory hypothesis H1: the G→V→R pipeline yields a lower regression‑causing change rate than the LLM‑only pipeline. The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in validator‑passing proportion, paired within task). Power assumptions were preregistered (target absolute reduction = 0.08 assuming baseline ≈ 0.20) and the analysis plan specified exact McNemar plus paired bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed=1729).
Deterministic task generation and selection. Tasks were produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. To avoid human selection bias we deterministically filtered and selected tasks: compute SHA‑256(intent_string), sort ascending, select first K=200 tasks after verifying preregistered validator coverage. All inclusions/exclusions and seeds are logged in execution/task_manifest.jsonl (artifact SHA‑256s in the manifest). Each task manifest contains initial_state, expected_final_state, intent, required_sequence, and workflow constraints used by the validator.
Shared initial generation and paired design. For each selected task a single generator call (shared_initial_generation) produced candidate_c. The baseline arm treated candidate_c as the suggested apply. The guarded arm ran the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) on the same candidate_c; if the validator flagged violations, the preregistered policy allowed a single repair call to the same model (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This paired, shared‑candidate design isolates the marginal verifier effect by holding generator randomness constant across arms and prevents generator adaptation to validator feedback during the paired comparison.
Model, provider, and deterministic verifier. The requested LLM was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: 1acce92558ed...), invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Provider call traces and per‑call hashes were archived under execution/provider_calls/*.json to detect stateful or cross‑condition contamination; the reconciliation audit confirms no cross‑condition cache reuse. The deterministic validator parses configuration text into structured commands and enforces preregistered workflow and dependency checks (examples: shutdown before MTU change; minimum‑up constraints). Scoring outputs record normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, and a boolean valid. Repair prompt text and repair_applied flags are archived; repair_applied==false for all guarded episodes in this run.
Execution and artifact accounting. Planned episodes = 2×K = 400 (baseline+guarded). Because generation was shared per task, host model calls used = 200 (one shared generation per task). Execution artifacts were archived and SHA‑256 hashed (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256: 3dfbe1b6...). The execution manifest documents start/complete timestamps, call counts, and per‑artifact hashes to enable replay and independent verification.

sections.discussion:
Interpretation: ceiling case vs practical utility. The observed degenerate null result—perfect validator compliance in both arms—reflects a ceiling case for this specific task/model/validator regime. When the generator proposals already satisfy the deterministic validator constraints, the verifier has no opportunity to change the binary apply outcome, and the repair stage is never exercised. This is an informative outcome: it documents a regime where G→V→R, as instantiated, produces no marginal benefit. It does not imply verifiers are unnecessary in general; production distributions include vendor idiosyncrasies, stateful interactions, feature gaps, and unexpected edge cases that can produce nontrivial generator errors.
Design lessons for future confirmatory evaluations. To empirically demonstrate verifier/repair value in a preregistered paired framework, experimenters should (a) sample task banks that intentionally include boundary or historical failure cases to raise baseline error rates, (b) evaluate multiple generator strengths (including weaker or smaller models) to produce nonzero baseline failure, (c) consider interactive generator–verifier protocols (allowing generator adaptation to verifier feedback) when measuring iterative improvement, and (d) ensure the validator realistically models operational checks; otherwise the test may produce ceiling artifacts similar to our run. Our archived per‑task difficulty labels and validator coverage matrix can be used to construct failure‑rich subpopulations for subsequent runs.
Threats to validity. Internal validity: protected through deterministic sampling, seed logging, and cryptographic hashing of artifacts (execution/* SHA‑256 manifest). Construct validity: hinges on whether validator.valid corresponds to operationally meaningful regression avoidance—the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 captures a set of workflow and dependency checks but does not simulate all production failures. External validity: limited by single‑model evaluation (gpt‑5‑mini), synthetic task pool, and forced shared_initial_generation design that prevents generator adaptation; results therefore do not generalize to other models or production intent distributions. Conclusion validity: initial power assumptions (baseline ≈0.20) were not met because observed baseline = 1.0; in such cases hypothesis tests correctly report nullity, but the design lacked the intended failure signal to detect verifier benefit.
Operational implications. Practitioners should not infer from this ceiling case that verifiers are redundant. Instead, apply our reproducible procedure to an operation‑representative task bank (including historical failure cases) and multiple generator qualities to assess whether verifier+repair reduces regressions under realistic conditions. The artifact bundle documents how to build such follow‑on evaluations: deterministic task generator parameters, per‑task difficulty annotations, validator traces, and call audit logs.
sections.conclusion: We ran a fully preregistered, paired evaluation comparing G→V→R and LLM‑only acceptance on K=200 deterministic NetOps tasks. Under the specific task/model/validator configuration the verifier had no marginal effect: both arms achieved 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar p = 1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00]. The repair loop was never invoked. This ceiling result is valuable: it highlights that to demonstrate verifier utility in confirmatory tests one must sample failure‑prone tasks or adjust generator/model choices to produce a nontrivial baseline error rate. We publish the full artifact bundle (preregistration, responses, provider traces, validator traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts with SHA‑256 hashes) to enable exact replay and to inform follow‑on preregistered studies that seek to quantify verifier and repair utility under operationally realistic conditions.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without additional experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task pool and deterministic sampling — external validity to production change intents and operator distributions is limited.
Primary outcome depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity to operational regressions; construct validity is tied to validator realism and coverage.
Ceiling effect: baseline success = 100% eliminated ability to demonstrate verifier/repair benefit under this design and sample.
Residual contamination (undetectable pretraining overlap) cannot be fully excluded despite hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv recorded no flagged items for this run.
